title: 1 Dollar, Federal Reserve Bank Note, United States, 1918
imageAlt: Photograph of 1918 One Dollar Banknote with Washington Portrait
story: Your story begins with an old dollar bill. Look closely—George Washington’s face is right there! This bill was made in 1918, long after he lived.

title: George Washington's Camp Chest
objectType: mess kit; camp chest; Equipment, Individual
description: Armies on campaign must carry with them much besides their weapons. At the time of the American Revolutionary War (1776-1781), various boxes and chests transported soldier's individual effects, wardrobes, official military payrolls, and other necessities. Camp chests or canteens as they were called in the 18th century, carried utensils and cooking apparatus to be used by officers and their staff when in the field during campaigns.
imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Camp Chest
story: Imagine the army getting ready to move. Washington brings this camp chest along. Inside are things he needs for cooking and eating on the journey.

title: George Washington's Uniform
objectType: coat; Man; Army; General Officer; Officer
description: This uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat, and knee breeches was worn by George Washington from 1789 until his death in 1799. The "small clothes," or breeches and waistcoat, date from the revolutionary period. The coat dates to 1789.
story: Washington gets dressed in his blue and tan army coat. People can spot their leader by the clothes he wears. Can you find both colors?

title: George Washington's Epaulettes
objectType: Epaulets, pair of; Insignia; Army; Holder, Epaulet; Officer
story: Something shiny rests on Washington’s shoulders. These gold pieces are called epaulettes. Artists put them in paintings of him, too.

title: George Washington Statue
description: This large statue shows George Washington sitting like a hero from ancient times. You can see it on the museum’s second floor.
story: You turn a corner and meet a giant Washington! An artist made him look like a hero from long ago. What do you notice about the way he sits?

title: George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
story: Here is the steel sword Washington wore while leading his army. It traveled with him during the Revolutionary War. Look for the long metal blade.

title: compass (surveyor's plain)
description: Legend has it that David Rittenhouse gave this compass to George Washington in 1782.
imageAlt: Photograph of a brass surveyor’s compass attributed to David Rittenhouse and associated with George Washington
story: Before he led an army, Washington worked as a surveyor. Surveyors measure land to make maps. This compass is part of his map-making story.

title: George Washington's Camp Stool
imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington’s Camp Stool
story: It is time for a rest at camp. Washington can unfold this small stool and sit down. Then it folds up again for the next trip.

title: Waistcoat worn by General George Washington
description: Collarless, buff wool waistcoat with a single row of fourteen metal buttons down the front, worn by General George Washington. Waistcoat is lined with linen, and has two front flap pockets, each with four buttons beneath flap. Although presented through the years as a uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat and breeches, the waistcoat and breeches are actually from an earlier uniform dating from the end of the Revolutionary War. The coat is slightly newer, dating from 1789
imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Waistcoat
story: Washington gets dressed for the day. Under his army coat he wears this wool waistcoat, a kind of vest. His outfit has more than one layer!

title: Breeches worn by General George Washington
description: Buff wool breeches worn by George Washington. Breeches have a two-button closure at waist and a waistband which is lined with linen. The front flap has a one-button closure on either side. There are two front pockets, with a watch pocket on the proper right side of the waistband. The legs have a five-button closure, with a separate tab and button on leg openings. Although presented through the years as a uniform consisting of coat, waistcoat and breeches, the waistcoat and breeches are actually from an earlier uniform dating from the end of the Revolutionary War. The coat is slightly newer, dating from 1789.
imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Breeches
story: Washington’s outfit needs pants, too. These wool breeches stop near the knees. Clothes looked a little different long ago.

title: 25 Cents, Tenino, Washington, United States, 1932
imageAlt: Photograph of Tenino 25-Cent Scrip with Washington Portrait
story: Many years after Washington lived, the town of Tenino needed money. It made its own paper money and put his face on it. Where else have you seen that face?

title: French Charleville Model 1763 Flintlock Musket, Surcharged "US"
objectType: musket; Firearms; Army; Flintlock; .70 In; Smooth Bore; Muzzle Load; Sa
story: The army Washington led needed long guns called muskets. He wanted these guns marked to show they belonged to the new United States. Why might an army mark its things?

title: Benjamin Lincoln's Sword
imageAlt: Photograph of Benjamin Lincoln’s Yorktown Sword
story: At Yorktown, the British army gave up. Washington asked another army leader, Benjamin Lincoln, to meet them. Lincoln carried this sword.

title: glasses, scissor
imageAlt: Photograph of Washington and Lafayette’s Scissor Glasses
story: Open, close! These glasses have handles that move like scissors. They are linked to Washington and his friend Lafayette.

title: Braddock Pistol
objectType: Firearms; Flintlock; .71 In; Muzzle Load; 00; Sa
imageAlt: Photograph of Braddock Pistol Used by Washington
story: A British general gave Washington this pistol. Washington carried it on later army trips. Now the museum keeps it safe so we can learn its story.

title: Commemorative Clothing Button, George Washington, 1789
description: Buttons such as this one reading “Long Live the President GW” were worn by supporters of George Washington during his first inauguration. There was no formal campaigning process during the first election. The framers of the Constitution presumed that the highly esteemed Washington would serve as the country’s first president, and he was elected unanimously by the Electoral College, with John Adams being elected as his vice president. There were no political parties at the time of Washington’s election, and though the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties began forming during his time in office, he remained officially non-partisan.
imageAlt: Photograph of “Long Live the President GW” Button
story: A big day arrives: Washington becomes the first U.S. president. People celebrate by wearing little brass buttons like this one. Can you see the letters GW?

title: Commemorative Clothing Button, George Washington, 1789
imageAlt: Photograph of Washington Inaugural Starburst Button
story: People want to celebrate Washington becoming president. Here is another button they wore, with a bright star design. Can you spot its shape?

title: George Washington
description: A silhouette is a picture made from a person’s outline. This one shows Washington from the side.
imageAlt: Photograph of Bache Silhouette of George Washington
story: An artist cuts Washington’s side view from a piece of paper. The dark shape is called a silhouette. Does it look like a shadow to you?

title: Piece of George Washington’s mahogany coffin
description: When George Washington’s remains were relocated to a new tomb in 1837, his family planned to make souvenirs from the mahogany covering of his lead-lined coffin. Its deteriorated condition made that idea unworkable, however, so they distributed small pieces of the wood. The note on this piece reads, “Washington’s Coffin presented to Mr. Saltonstall by a nephew, + namesake of Washington residing at Mount Vernon.”
imageAlt: Photograph of Piece of Washington’s Mahogany Coffin
story: After Washington died, people saved this tiny piece of wood from an older coffin made for him. They kept it to remember him. Even a small object can hold a big story.
